title: The Lord’s preface warns the world and vouches for his servants
setting: Joseph Smith received this revelation on 1 November 1831 at Hiram, Ohio, during a conference of elders. The elders had met to plan a published book of his revelations, the Book of Commandments. Minutes say the revelation came during a break between the conference sessions. William McLellin later recalled that the conference rejected a preface drafted by Oliver Cowdery, Sidney Rigdon, and McLellin himself. According to McLellin, Joseph then dictated this preface a few sentences at a time while Rigdon wrote.
summary: The revelation opens with a voice calling all people, near and far, to listen. It says disciples chosen in the last days will carry a warning to everyone. It calls itself the Lord’s preface to the book of his commandments. It charges that people have strayed from God’s ordinances and broken his everlasting covenant. It says the Lord, knowing the coming calamity, called Joseph Smith so that “the weak and the simple” could proclaim the gospel. It says the commandments came to servants in their weakness, so their errors could be corrected and their humility rewarded. It calls the church “the only true and living church” and promises forgiveness to those who repent. It ends by telling readers to search these commandments, which it says will all be fulfilled.

contextNote.title: Why publish revelations given to weak men
contextNote.text: A book of revelations faced an obvious objection: the men who received them were ordinary and flawed. Verse 24 answers it directly. It says the commandments came “in their weakness, after the manner of their language” so servants could understand. Verses 25–28 then list the purpose: errors made known, sinners chastened, the humble made strong. Verse 38 states the other side: the word is “the same” whether the Lord or his servants speak it. In this preface, the servants’ weakness is part of how the revelations came, not a flaw the book hides.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson on section 1 teaches that the Lord uses “the weak and the simple” to do his work. In verses 24–28, what four outcomes does the Lord promise for servants who err, seek wisdom, sin, or are humble?
reviewNote: Read all 39 verses. Official heading gives Hiram, Ohio, 1 November 1831, at a special conference planning publication of the revelations. JSP historical introduction read: minutes say it came by inspiration during a recess; the account of the rejected Cowdery–Rigdon draft and Rigdon as scribe comes from William McLellin’s recollection about fifty years later, so it is attributed to him. Fact-check 2026-10-12: setting now says McLellin recalled drafting the rejected preface with Cowdery and Rigdon (JSP), not Cowdery and Rigdon alone. Fact-check 2026-10-12: summary sentences on Joseph’s call and the servants’ weakness now attributed to the text.
